segments.say: One of the most common fears about social media is that it locks us inside bubbles. We follow people who agree with us, algorithms feed us more of what we like, and over time, we stop seeing anything else. Our views harden, we grow more extreme, and we lose the ability to understand people on the other side. It's a compelling story. The evidence is more tangled.

It helps to separate two ideas that often get mixed up. An echo chamber is a space in which people mostly hear their own views repeated, often because they choose to. A filter bubble is a similar situation caused by algorithms, which show us more of what they predict we'll like. The first is about our choices, and the second is about the machine's.
Both ideas are plausible, and both have been argued strongly. But they also make testable predictions, and researchers have begun to test them.

show.title: Two explanations
items: Echo chamber: we pick people who agree with us
Filter bubble: algorithms pick content for us
Each could make views more extreme
Each is hard to measure

segments.say: In 2015, a team at Facebook, led by Eytan Bakshy, with Solomon Messing and Lada Adamic, analysed the news that over ten million American users saw and clicked on. They wanted to know how much of what we see is shaped by our friends, by the algorithm, and by our own choices.

They found that people's friends tended to share news that matched their own politics, so the friends' selection already narrowed what people saw. The ranking algorithm reduced the share of opposing views a little further, and people's own clicks narrowed it more. In their analysis, individual choice was the biggest factor, with the algorithm playing a smaller role, though critics pointed out that the data came from the company itself.

show.what: Exposure to ideologically diverse news and opinion on Facebook

segments.say: It's a good example of why this debate is hard to settle. The data is from the platform, the analysis was run by its own scientists, and the results suggest that the platform's algorithm is less to blame than the choices of users. Some outside researchers questioned the framing and the sampling, and others argued the findings had been presented in too reassuring a way.

show.title: Facebook users in the news exposure study
show.label: American users who shared their political affiliation on the platform

segments.say: Even so, the finding fits an old pattern in psychology. People prefer information that fits what they already think, a tendency called confirmation bias. They follow people like themselves, which is called homophily. Those tendencies shape a feed before any algorithm touches it. The algorithm may then amplify what we've already started.

So what happens if you deliberately break the bubble? In 2018, Chris Bail and his colleagues at Duke University tried it. They recruited one thousand six hundred and fifty-two Twitter users in the United States, who identified as Democrats or Republicans, and paid them to follow a bot that retweeted messages from elected officials, organisations and opinion leaders on the opposite side.

For about a month, these users saw a stream of content from the other side. The researchers measured their attitudes before and afterwards. Republicans who followed a liberal bot became more conservative, by a modest but clear amount. Democrats who followed a conservative bot showed a small shift in a more liberal direction, though this one wasn't statistically convincing.

show.who: Bail, Argyle, Brown, Bumpus, Chen, Hunzaker, Lee, Mann, Merhout & Volfovsky
show.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2018
show.what: Exposure to opposing views on social media can increase political polarization

segments.say: This was a surprise to many people. It suggests that simply being shown opposing views isn't enough, and may backfire when the views appear in an angry or mocking form, as they often do online. The way we meet the other side may matter as much as whether we do.

show.title: What the Duke experiment suggests
items: Seeing the other side did not soften views
Republicans became more conservative
Democrats showed a smaller, uncertain shift
Exposure alone is not understanding

segments.say: As always, we should hold this loosely. The study involved a particular set of people, a particular platform, and a particular month. The researchers themselves stressed that their findings don't prove that exposure always polarises. But they challenge the comfortable idea that a bit more exposure would fix things.

Perhaps the most ambitious tests came around the 2020 American elections. In collaboration with Meta, a group of academics designed several large experiments, in which some users were randomly given a different version of Facebook or Instagram. The results were published in 2023, in Science and Nature, and were widely discussed.

In one experiment, tens of thousands of users were switched from the usual algorithmic feed to a simple chronological feed, showing posts in order of time. The change reduced the time they spent on the platform, and altered what they saw, with less political content and fewer posts from like-minded sources, though more content from untrustworthy sources. But after three months, it didn't measurably change their political attitudes or polarisation.

show.who: Guess, Malhotra, Pan, Barberá, Allcott & others
show.what: How do social media feed algorithms affect attitudes and behavior in an election campaign?

segments.say: This is a result that surprised many people. Even changing the algorithm for months didn't shift beliefs in a measurable way. The researchers noted that the experiment ran for three months, during an election, and that the effects of years of use might differ. But it suggests that polarisation has deeper roots than the feed alone.

Careful scientists don't conclude from this that feeds don't matter. They conclude that the simplest story, in which an algorithm is the main driver of political division, isn't supported by the best experiments so far.

show.title: What the 2020 experiments suggest
items: Switching to chronological feeds changed what people saw
It did not change political attitudes in three months
Reducing reshares also had limited effects
Polarisation has many causes besides feeds

segments.say: Two jars, two colours, and a few marbles rolling in between. It's a picture of the debate: separate groups, some movement between them, and a long argument about what, exactly, keeps the marbles apart.

If you'd like to understand people who disagree with you, the research suggests that the form of the encounter matters. Calm, curious questions work better than public arguments, which tend to harden both sides. Looking for even one point of honest agreement lowers the temperature. And moving a heated thread to a private message takes away the audience, and with it a lot of the performance. It won't convert anyone. But it can turn a fight into a conversation, which is a good deal more useful.

show.title: A better way to meet the other side
items: Ask a question before offering an opinion
Look for something you can honestly agree with
Avoid quote-posting someone to mock them
Move a heated thread into a private conversation

segments.say: Four terms about bubbles. An echo chamber is a space where we mostly hear our own views. A filter bubble is the same thing produced by algorithms. Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour what fits what we already believe. And homophily is the tendency to befriend people who are like us.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Echo chamber
Filter bubble
Confirmation bias
Homophily

segments.say: If you want to climb out of any bubble, the research suggests that anger isn't the way in. A calmer approach is to ask someone on the other side a real question, and to listen to the answer. That's slow, and it's rarely done online. But it's the kind of exposure that studies of conversation suggest actually works.

So what did we learn? That echo chambers and filter bubbles are different ideas. That users' own choices shaped exposure a lot in a large study. That following the other side, in an angry setting, didn't soften views. And that changing the algorithm for three months didn't shift attitudes.
Next, we'll look at memory. What does it do to your recollection of an event when you photograph it? And what happens to what we know when the answer is always one search away?
